passages.t: ‘Hear this, all you peoples’: no one can buy a life from death
passages.happening:
This psalm is a teacher speaking. “Hear this, all you peoples; listen, all inhabitants of the world, both low and high, rich and poor alike” (verses 1 and 2). He promises wisdom and a ‘riddle’ sung with a harp (verses 3 and 4).

His riddle is a question. “Why should I fear in times of trouble, when wicked usurpers surround me?” (verse 5). These are people who “trust in their wealth and boast in their great riches” (verse 6).

The answer is death. Money cannot buy anyone out of it. “No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God. For the redemption of his soul is costly, and never can payment suffice” (verses 7 and 8). The wise die, and so do the foolish, and both “leave their wealth to others” (verse 10).

Then a line that comes back at the end. “But a man, despite his wealth, cannot endure; he is like the beasts that perish” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is a wisdom psalm, like the book of Proverbs (the book page explains the kinds of psalm). It speaks to everyone, not only to Israel.

‘Redeem’ and ‘ransom’ were words of law. In some cases a life that was lost under the law could be bought back with money: “he may redeem his life by paying the full amount demanded of him” (Exodus 21:30). The psalm says death is not like that. No price is high enough.

The rich often named their lands after themselves, hoping their name would last (verse 11). A grave was the only house that lasted.

The Hebrew of a few verses here, especially 11, 13 and 14, is hard to read. Bibles put those lines in different ways. The main point is clear.
passages.later:
Jesus told of a rich man who built bigger barns and died that night. “But God said to him, ‘You fool! This very night your life will be required of you’” (Luke 12:20). Paul says, “For we brought nothing into the world, so we cannot carry anything out of it” (1 Timothy 6:7).

The psalm says no one can pay the ransom for another. Jesus said he came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). What no brother could pay, Christians believe he paid.
passages.asks:
The psalm is not against having money. It is against trusting it. Its question is simple: what are you counting on that death will take away?

It also sets the poor free from fear. The rich man's power ends where everyone's does.

passages.t: ‘Death will be their shepherd’, and ‘God will redeem my life from Sheol’
passages.happening:
The self-confident are pictured as a flock. “Like sheep they are destined for Sheol. Death will be their shepherd” (verse 14).

Then the turn of the whole psalm. “But God will redeem my life from Sheol, for He will surely take me to Himself” (verse 15). What no human payment could do, God will do.

So the teacher gives his advice. “Do not be amazed when a man grows rich, when the splendor of his house increases. For when he dies, he will carry nothing away” (verses 16 and 17).

The last line repeats verse 12 with one change. “A man who has riches without understanding is like the beasts that perish” (verse 20). It is not riches that make the difference. It is understanding.
passages.hearers:
‘Death will be their shepherd’ turns Psalm 23 upside down. There the LORD is the shepherd who leads through the dark valley. Here death leads the flock down.

Sheol was the place of the dead. The book page explains what the psalmists knew, and did not yet know, of life after death. It quotes verse 15 as one of the brighter lines.

‘Take me’ is the same Hebrew verb used of Enoch: “Enoch walked with God, and then he was no more, because God had taken him away” (Genesis 5:24). Psalm 73 uses it too: “and later receive me in glory” (Psalm 73:24).
passages.later: Paul calls the risen Jesus the firstfruits of those who have died (1 Corinthians 15:20): the first of a harvest still to come. For Christians, verse 15 gets its full shape at the empty tomb.
passages.hard: Does verse 15 mean life with God after death, or only rescue from an early death? Readers differ, and the book page sets out both. Some think it means being kept from dying now. Others point out that the whole psalm says everyone dies, wise and foolish alike. A short delay would not answer the riddle. So the faithful must have a different end. Many readers hold that the psalmist hoped for more than he could fully see.
passages.asks:
The difference in this psalm is not between rich and poor. It is between those whose shepherd is death and those whom God takes to himself.

Verse 20 asks a quiet question. Do you have ‘understanding’ about what you own? Hold it the way someone holds a thing they will have to leave.
